hook: We killed {ritual} at {company}. No {artifact}. No {artifact}. No \"{cliché test}\" questions." — or comp-forward variant: "We're hiring a {role}. And we're paying ${range} to find our next killer.
skeleton: The kill statement + staccato list of banished rituals
Why the ritual is now meaningless (a real shift — e.g., AI assistants break assessments)
What we actually select for, stated as identity ("we're building products, not algorithms")
The replacement process, numbered and concrete (projects shown, reference calls)

example_text:
We killed LeetCode at Virio.

No online assessments. No whiteboard problems. No "reverse a binary tree" questions. With AI coding assistants everywhere, technical rounds are borderline meaningless now. Anyone can pass them with the right setup of ChatGPT + Claude + Cluely.

We're not building algorithms at Virio. We're building a product that actual customers pay for and use every day.

I don't need someone who's solved 500 LeetCode hard problems. I need someone who can ship a feature from idea → design → code → production in a week.

This is what we do instead to find real builders:

1️⃣ Previous projects: Show us what you've actually built and shipped.
2️⃣ Reference calls with your past teammates: We want to hear how you actually performed on a team, not how well you prepped for an interview.

That's it.

If you can build, iterate fast, and care about the end user experience more than the perfect algorithm - we should talk.

Drop a comment here if you're interested, let's build real products together.

name: Counterintuitive-investment story

skeleton: Shock/contradiction hook
The overlooked problem or expectation everyone holds, with one hard number (CO₂ ppm, capacity %)
The mechanism: why the conventional choice is wrong (short, factual lines)
The decision + named specifics (the building, the expert, the sq ft, the desk math)
The anticipated objection voiced ("people ask me, why would a startup invest in this?")

We raised $38M. Kept our cramped office. Hit 300% capacity. Now we're moving in a space we designed.

When we closed our Series B, everyone expected us to upgrade immediately.
We didn't.

We kept adding desks.
Squeezed in phone booths.
Put people wherever they fit.

At one point, we had 30 people and 1 bathroom.
We hit 300% over capacity.

Now we're moving into a space 5x larger.
Every detail we couldn't control before, we designed this time.

We didn't stay in the old office just to be scrappy.

It was about priorities.
Build the product.
Hire the team.
Then build the space.

We're ready now.

name: Culture line-in-the-sand
archetype: polarizing culture manifesto that deliberately filters the audience
hook: Quoted outrage or inverted cliché: "\"SHOVE YOUR JOB UP YOUR AZZ\" — worst and best line I heard from a candidate." / "We at {company} don't believe in 996 — we only work when we want to work.
skeleton: Polarizing hook (a quote, a heresy, or a both-sides paradox)
Name the practice plainly, no euphemism ("yes, we do 996, 9am-9pm, 6 days")
Stage the two reactions the post will get (pre-empting the comments)
The filter logic: who this is for, who it isn't, and why that's the point
Honest concession beat (the cost, the caveat — "we know this isn't sustainable forever")
Self-selection close ("if you read this and thought X — we should talk") — follow-level CTA max
example_text:
"SHOVE YOUR JOB UP YOUR AZZ"

Worst and best line I heard from a candidate I interviewed. Yes, we do 996 which means working 9am-9pm, 6 days a week.

It's funny because there are two extremes of how people react when I say that. They either say:

> "you're a slave, a victim of capitalism and hustle culture, your CEO is exploiting you!!! shove that job up your azz"

or:

> "oh man I do that already lol"

The reason why we keep it transparent is because we're looking for those people.

People who've run their own business or started their own startup get it. Building something from nothing is extremely hard. It demands sacrifice, obsession, and an unreasonable amount of hours.

That doesn't mean you're literally chained to your desk for 12 hours a day. It means putting in your best effort - 100%, 120%. But saying "996" is the best filter.

We're not trying to convince anyone this lifestyle is for them. If your gut reaction is the first one - respect. Genuinely. That boundary is valid.
But if you read 996 and thought "yeah that's just Tuesday" - we should talk.

And look - we know this isn't sustainable forever. As the team grows, the pace will change. 996 is an early-stage reality, not a long-term culture. The goal is to earn the right to slow down by building something that works first.

After being head-down for the last 4 years building Wispr and raising over $81M in funding, I think it's time to reintroduce myself.

Hi, my name is Sahaj.

Before building Wispr, I spent my sophomore year of undergrad at Stanford treating research like a mini-PhD. 50 hours a week in the lab while neglecting most of my actual coursework.

What was I spending these 50 hours a week on? Researching and writing one of the earliest papers at Stanford on diffusion-based generative models.

Back then, we had this bet: if you could represent image data in a more intuitive way, the model would be way easier to train and work better.

It barely worked when we were building it. Now it's the foundation of every major image generation model.

From Jersey kid doing math competitions and neuroscience research on rhesus macaques, to quant trading (hated it - people coin-flipped $20 bills for fun because it nets zero), to Google ML fairness work that's now deployed in YouTube.

Between undergrad quarters, I walked the Camino de Santiago, 500 miles across northern Spain. Did a 10-day silent Vipassana retreat.

The big takeaway: learning via experience, wisdom not just knowledge, is the only way to actually understand anything.

That pushed me to join my first startup.

Optical computing company, $100M raised, eventually shut down. Learned a critical lesson: I could see the product was off track but wasn't senior enough to make the case for pivoting.

Coming out of that, I knew what mattered: solving a problem I actually care about, with someone I love working with. [...]

Looking forward to the next 4 years with our amazing team

We just hired Clay's first Head of Sales. Here's an inside look at what the interview process looked like (and the take-home prompts I think other teams might find helpful):

As you can imagine, I know a lot of sales leaders! In fact, it's my day job to meet them. So you can believe me when I say I knew Becca Lindquist was special the first time we met.

Let's start with what I was looking for:

1. Philosophical alignment: We approach sales differently at Clay. We hire GTM engineers to sell Clay in a highly consultative process that prizes product knowledge and customer empathy over traditional sales backgrounds. We have a low-pressure, fit-oriented approach.

2. People leadership and process: Our org is scaling quickly, and we need someone to come in and build a system that can help us scale, not just win based off force of will and charisma.

Here was the interview process:

First, I set up multiple behavioral interviews for Becca on sales process and people management with sales leaders at customers we trusted (thank you Dannie Herzberg and Stevie Case!). Then we did a deep dive interview where we went through every role in her career in great detail. We also asked her to complete a take-home with the following instructions:

- Current State: We'll share Gong calls, written docs, closed/won + pipeline data, and would love to see what you come back with in terms of top 5 opp[ortunities...]

Anthropic's argument isn't just "ads are annoying." It's that AI conversations are fundamentally different to search or social. People share more with a chatbot than they ever would with Google. Ads in that context don't just interrupt, they erode trust.

Thank you TIME for naming me as  one of the “Titans” on your first-ever TIME100 Creator List!!! I am deeply honored!

As a 56-year-old woman, I am also proud to be one of the oldest people on the list, not in spite of my age but because of it.

It proves what I say to you every week on The Mel Robbins Podcast: it’s never too late and you’re never too old to start creating the life you’ve always wanted.

When I started posting online back in 2012,  I wasn’t “trying” to go viral. I was just trying to book a few speaking gigs so I could pay our bills and get out of debt. That’s it. Just me, a married mother of 3, hoping someone would take me seriously and hire me.

In the beginning, every post felt cringey.

Every. Single. Post.

I’d spend hours crafting the “perfect” thing. I’d have to give myself a 10-minute pep talk before hitting “post,” and when I finally did it, I’d then check it obsessively. Five minutes would pass, and if the likes or comments weren’t what I was hoping for, my insecurity would kick in and I’d delete it.

I created hundreds of draft posts...and they would just sit there, staring back at me for years.

So here’s my message to you:

There is no secret formula.

It’s you against you. The only difference between you and most of us on the #TIME100Creators list is that, despite how cringey it felt in the beginning, we got started and kept going. Day after day. Year after year. And in my case, 13 years later, here I am…  And that’s how you’re going to change your life, too.

So start now. Even if you’re afraid of what people might think. 

In fact, just use The Let Them Theory.

If they roll their eyes? Let Them. 
If they judge you? Let Them.

You’re not creating for them...
You’re building something for YOU.

You don’t need to be perfect. You need to begin.

Your future self will thank you, and so will I.

And in case no one else tells you, as your friend, I want to tell you that I love you and I believe in you and your ability to create a better life. Forcing yourself to do the things that you don’t feel like doing is exactly how you do it. Xo Mel

And a huge shoutout to everyone on the list and who is inspired to be creating 💚

Do you know how to perform CPR (Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation)?

1) Safety First: Ensure the scene is safe for both you and the victim. Look out for any potential hazards.
2) Check Responsiveness: Gently tap the person's shoulder and shout, "Are you okay?" If there's no response, it's time to act.
3) Call for Help: Dial emergency services or direct someone else to do so. Quick professional intervention is crucial.
4) Begin CPR: Position Your Hands: Place the heel of one hand on the center of the person's chest. Place your other hand on top and interlock your fingers.
5) Give Compressions: Press down hard and fast, at least 2 inches deep, and at a rate of 100-120 compressions per minute. Allow the chest to rise fully between compressions.
6) Open the Airway: Tilt the head back slightly and lift the chin.
7) Provide Rescue Breaths (if trained): Pinch the nose shut, place your mouth fully over the person's mouth, and blow to make the chest rise. Give 2 breaths, each lasting about 1 second.
8) Continue CPR: Keep performing cycles of chest compressions and rescue breaths until medical professionals arrive or the person begins to show signs of life.

I'm writing this post as a final, last ditch effort. After 8 months and 825+ applications, this is the only thing I haven't tried. This is my cry for help. My life as I know it is ending. My savings that I was responsible to have are gone. Everything I've built is falling apart and I am very close to losing everything.

I don't need new strategies. I've changed resumes, messaged recruiters, had direct referrals, contacted headhunters, tried roles within my network, outside. If you can think of it, I've tried it. There's no "strategy" that will work for me.

If you are a hiring manager or a direct recruiter this message is for you. I'm confident enough to know what I can bring. You will not find a harder worker, and I have results to prove it. I bring innovative solution, creative ideas, and stability to teams in need, as a Scrum Master or a Project Manager. I have a background in software engineering, so I can be a bridge between high ranking stakeholders and dev teams. I have a passion for finishing complex projects, many times multiple at a time, and seeing things through from start to finish.

Everything that has come close has just been false hope, and it has destroyed what confidence I still had in myself. Some may view this as "unprofessional" but the right organization for me would see this and be understanding. I didn't ask to be put in this position. I loved my job, and they unceremoniously dismissed me at a moments notice over a 1 way video call. I'm not sure what deity I pissed off but I can't get anything going for myself. I have valuable experience and a valuable education, I just need someone to realize that.

So here's what I'm asking for: connect me DIRECTLY with someone who is hiring for a job in my field, Scrum Master, Project Manager, or anything similar. I don't need links to job boards, I don't need links to roles with no human connection. If those worked, I wouldn't be writing this now. And no, I don't need "words of encouragement". I'm sorry if that comes across as rude or mean, but nice words will not pay my bills.

Thank you for taking the time to read this. I wish none of this had to be written. This is an extremely vulnerable post for me, but my life is at a tipping point and I can't wait any longer. Please help.

example_text:
Every once in a while in my job, you get to witness products that feel like they are past their prime. At one point, they were the talk of the town and then innovation gradually slowed down and competition took the lead. These are moments where we fail our customers. 

But then, a resurgence of innovation occurs, and the team does the impossible to innovate and bring the product back to its glory days. This is when the market is skeptical at first, but loyal customers give the team another chance to prove themselves. And the team takes on the challenge. 

One such example at Cisco was our Firewall business. For the longest time, we had let the product be ignored. Quality had dropped and so had innovation. But a few years ago, credit to one of our Board members and a highly motivated team, we decided that the Firewall is the core foundation of our Security offering. The team knew this wouldn’t be easy. Not only did the quality of the product need massive improvement but we would have to innovate non-linearly. The team not only delivered but did so in a way that made it one of the most remarkable turnarounds I have witnessed. As an aerospace engineer, former NASA rocket scientist, and the first Bahamian to fly to space, I care deeply about science, sustainability, and what this mission actually represented.

For ya'll who think it was short, traveling at 2,300 MPH makes you feel a way 😉 So let's break it down:

1. Purpose of the mission:

Yes, Blue Origin's New Shepard is suborbital—but this mission made history in more ways than one. I served as the science payload operator for the first-ever HBCU-led research project to fly aboard New Shepard, developed in partnership with Winston-Salem State University (WSSU). The mission also marked a first for BioServe Space Technologies, whose Fluid Processing Apparatus (FPA) hardware was flown to qualify it for future use in orbit.

In addition to advancing plant biology research by examining how crops like chickpeas and sweet potatoes grow in microgravity to support future food security. I also wore a BioButton as part of a NASA-funded study led by TRISH (Translational Research Institute for Space Health) to better understand how women's bodies respond to spaceflight. This work is essential for future deep space exploration, where gender-specific data is still significantly lacking. Not tourism. Research.

2. Climate impact:

Rockets do have an environmental cost just like cargo ships, long-haul flights, and even your average data center. But this wasn't just about one flight. The long game is reusability. New Shepard is fully reusable, and part of developing cleaner, more sustainable launch vehicles something we need if we want to monitor climate, deliver satellites, or support Earth-observation missions. And by the way, many climate-monitoring tools rely on space infrastructure.

3. The role of private people:

I left NASA to found two companies focused on education and equity. Through LINGO, we've brought STEM access to over 10,000 students worldwide, including in The Bahamas. The goal isn't just to go to space it's to bring what we learn back home.

4. Private vs. public investment:

Let's not pretend private sector innovation doesn't play a role in societal advancement. Commercial spaceflight delivers satellites for disaster tracking, global internet, GPS and agriculture monitoring to name a few benefits. It's space for the benefit of Earth.

5. Marketing and representation:

Representation isn't just about optics it's about access. As a Black woman and first-generation Bahamian-American, I didn't grow up thinking space was for me. This mission sent a powerful message: that science isn't reserved for the elite few. It belongs to all of us. And if one young girl saw me and thought maybe I could study engineering, I consider that a mission success.

Yes, be critical. Always. But don't dismiss the science, the significance, or the opportunity to inspire and inform 🙏🏽🚀💙

hook: The interview is for a {role} at {company}." — then straight into dialogue
skeleton: One-line scene set naming the role and company
Interviewer question (the naive framing)
Candidate answer (crisp, correct, quotable)
Escalating follow-ups (3–4 rounds), each punching a common misconception
The synthesis answer — the mental model, stated plainly
Optional resource block or takeaway line

examples.meta: Sourav Verma, 1,143 reactions / 33 comments, Nov 2025 (GenAI engineer interview at Cohere)
Paweł Huryn, 4,175 reactions, Jun 2025 (step-by-step agent build, resource-dense variant)

example_text:
The interview is for a Generative AI Engineer role at Cohere.

Interviewer: "Your client complains that the LLM keeps losing track of earlier details in a long chat. What's happening?"

You: "That's a classic context window problem.
 Every LLM has a fixed memory limit - say 8k, 32k, or 200k tokens.
 Once that's exceeded, earlier tokens get dropped or compressed, and the model literally forgets."

Interviewer: "So you just buy a bigger model?"

You: "You can, but that's like using a megaphone when you need a microphone.
A larger context window costs more, runs slower, and doesn't always reason better."

Interviewer: "Then how do you manage long-term memory?"

You:
  1. Summarization memory - periodically condense earlier chat segments into concise summaries.
  2. Vector memory - store older context as embeddings; retrieve only the relevant pieces later.
  3. Hybrid memory - combine summaries for continuity and retrieval for precision.

Interviewer: "So you're basically simulating memory?"

You: "Yep.
LLMs are stateless by design.
You build memory on top of them - a retrieval layer that acts like long-term memory.
Otherwise, your chatbot becomes a goldfish."

Interviewer: "And how do you know if the memory strategy works?"

You: "When the system recalls context correctly without bloating cost or latency.
 If a user says, 'Remind me what I told you last week,' and it answers from stored embeddings - that's memory done right."

Interviewer: "So context management isn't a model issue - it's an architecture issue?"

You: "Exactly.
 Most think 'context length' equals intelligence.
 But true intelligence is recall with relevance - not recall with redundancy."

name: Magic demo
archetype: teach a principle by showing how a named company made something "boring" spectacular
hook: Your \"boring\" {thing}? It's pure magic. [watch/look at this {unexpected analog}]
skeleton: Reframe hook (boring → magic) + an unexpected analog (a physics teacher, a street vendor)
The analog's trick in two lines (show, don't explain)
Bridge: "Your {ICP's thing}? Same story."
Numbered how-to (3 steps, each with 2–3 sub-bullets)
The named-company proof: "Look at {company}:" — what they did, concrete numbers, and the outcome ("biggest software IPO in history")
Challenge close: tell the reader to try it on their most boring feature

examples.meta: Moshe Pesach, 7,861 reactions / 135 comments, May 2025 (Snowflake made data warehousing exciting)
Sourav Verma, 1,143 reactions, Nov 2025 (Cohere interview dialogue as a teaching device)

example_text:
Your "boring" solution? It's pure magic.
[Watch this Physics teacher]

That physics teacher just made basic principles fascinating.

How?

Not by explaining the theory.
By showing how it works.

Your B2B solution?
It's the same story.

- Reveal the mechanics
- Demonstrate each step

2. Make It Real
- Live demonstrations
- Behind-the-scenes
- Real results

3. Show the Magic

- Share insider tricks
- Reveal the "how"

Made data warehousing exciting

Instead of: "Enterprise data solution"

They showed:

- Live data sharing between companies

Pick your most "boring" feature.
Break down how it works.
Make someone say, "Wow."

Remember:
To the right audience, HOW you do it is magic.

name: Milestone announcement + team credit
archetype: proud first-person announcement of a company milestone (research published, launch, record) with findings/details and named team credit
hook: NEW {company} {thing} ON {topic}" caps hook / "I am proud to share that {company} {milestone}.
skeleton: Caps or pride hook naming the company and milestone
Scale line (4.3M nights, 15K members — the numbers that make it real)
The substance: findings/features as dash bullets (3–4, each specific)
"So what?" — one-line practical implication for the reader
Why only this company could do it (the moat line)
Named congratulations to the people behind it, titles included

examples.meta: Will Ahmed, 4,430 reactions / 191 comments, Apr 2025 (WHOOP study in Nature Communications; SVP credited by name)
Avi Chawla, 2,996 reactions, Aug 2025 ("built by the team behind LightRAG")

example_text:
NEW WHOOP RESEARCH ON EXERCISE & SLEEP

I am proud to share that WHOOP research has just been published in Nature Portfolio's Nature Communications. Our study analyzed 4.3 million nights of sleep across nearly 15,000 WHOOP members to answer a simple but important question: does working out at night hurt your sleep?

Here's what we found:
-Strenuous evening workouts can delay sleep onset, shorten sleep duration, and reduce sleep quality.
-Elevated nocturnal heart rate and decreased heart rate variability were observed post high-strain evening exercise.
-Importantly, workouts concluding at least 4 hours before bedtime showed no negative impact on sleep.

So what? If you're training hard but not sleeping well, *when* you work out may matter just as much as how you work out.

This is one of the largest studies ever published on exercise and sleep - and it's only possible because of continuous WHOOP data and our commitment to research that improves human performance.

Congratulations to Emily Capodilupo, our SVP of Research, Algorithms, and Data, and her team, as well as our collaborators at Monash and Harvard.

Full article in Nature: https://lnkd.in/e6MXE85u

name: Named-rival rebuttal
archetype: a named exec/company makes a public claim; the author counters it with their own company's data
hook: This past weekend {company}'s CEO shared that {claim}." / "{policy} isn't the solution to the real problem: {reframe}.
skeleton: Hook restating the named claim neutrally (date-stamped)
"At {our company} we're seeing the opposite:" — the counter-signal
The data: study scope, n, what was measured, what it found (2–4 lines)
Reframe: what the claim gets wrong about the underlying problem
Principle close ("this moment demands more") — no gloating

examples.meta: Annie Dean, 8,063 reactions / 281 comments, Apr 2024 (Atlassian data vs Nike CEO)
Annie Dean, 11,875 reactions / 592 comments, Sep 2024 (vs Amazon RTO memo, citing Airbnb's Chesky)

example_text:
This past weekend Nike's CEO shared that remote work was hurting innovation.

At Atlassian we're seeing signals that distributed teams are * more * innovative.

We analyzed data from 4,000 shipit teams — shipit is our 2x annual internal hackathon — across 8 different shipit hackathons since 2021. We found that distributed (vs local) shipit teams were more diverse (range of skills, members spread across more crafts, more levels) and that they were more likely to produce a demo and receive a higher rank by voters.

When we commit to doing it well, organizing our work online-first (vs office-first) is often * better *. "We're struggling to innovate" is an admission that a company isn't evolving how work gets done, not evidence that the office drives innovation.

name: News clapback

What the thing actually is/does (the context critics skip)

examples.meta: Will Ahmed, 5,260 reactions / 408 comments, Jul 2025 (WHOOP vs FDA warning letter)
Eduardo Ordax, 4,766 reactions / 282 comments, Aug 2025 (Copilot Studio agents wrecked at DEFCON)

example_text:
The FDA just sent WHOOP a warning letter about our Blood Pressure Insights feature. Here's why that's misguided, why it undermines innovation in the United States, and why we're not backing down.

Blood Pressure Insights by Whoop is a wellness feature. It gives members a daily estimate of their blood pressure range, based on passive, overnight data, to help optimize sleep, recovery, and performance. It's accurate and non-invasive.

It does not diagnose any condition. It's clearly labeled not for medical use. In fact, anyone accessing the app is required to go through an in-depth onboarding where they acknowledge that they know the device should not be used for medical purposes.

Here's what's frustrating: the FDA claims any display of blood pressure — regardless of disclaimers — requires medical clearance. That's like saying your wearable shouldn't show your heart rate because someone might think they have tachycardia if it's too high.

Heart rate and respiratory monitors are regulated under 21 C.F.R. §§ 870.2300 and 868.2375, yet wearables can show that data for wellness. Blood pressure is no different. Peer-reviewed research confirms its relevance for wellness. There's no reason to treat it differently.

Intended use is what matters - and the law agrees. The 21st Century Cures Act makes clear: Tools that support healthy lifestyles and don't diagnose or treat disease aren't medical devices. Blood Pressure Insights meets that standard.

We've gone above and beyond to design this feature responsibly:
-We tell members: this is not a medical device
-It does not diagnose hypertension or any other condition
-It accurately estimates your blood pressure range every day as measured
-We require members to proactively acknowledge that this device is not a medical feature
-It's based on passive overnight trends - not clinical readings

We even invited the FDA to review the feature, the science, and the disclaimers. They declined to review all the details. Now they just want us to remove it. We are going to fight for our members' access to their data.

To be clear, Whoop supports the FDA's right to regulate medical devices. We spent years getting FDA clearance for our ECG feature that detects AFib. That's a medical device. We follow the rules. Blood Pressure Insights, however, isn't a medical device. And we won't let regulatory overreach dictate how people access their own health data.

Worth noting, this is a US specific disagreement. Blood Pressure Insights by Whoop has been received favorably in 50+ markets around the world.

This isn't just about Whoop. It's about your right to understand your body and your health. It's about giving Americans access to health and wellness data. We'll fight this. Because the data can be measured accurately, and it belongs to you.

Alexandra Tachalova, 6,933 reactions, May 2025 (Semrush 12-person era origin story)

example_text:
In 2020, ALDI infamously copied our flagship beer.

ALDI - famous for its "inspired by" products - launched "Anti-Establishment IPA", a blatant copy of Punk IPA.

Same branding.
Same product description.
No shame 😅.

The normal response here would be to enter a legal battle, spending millions on fees to try and win a war.

Instead, we sent a tweet:

👉 "I wonder what ALDI would call Elvis Juice?"

Then, we took it a step further—announcing a new BrewDog beer called YALDI IPA.

Our message? Let's have some fun.

ALDI fired back: "We would have gone with ALD IPA. Send us a crate and we'll talk?"

So we did. We even redesigned the label to match their suggestion.

Within days, what could have been a corporate war turned into the most unexpected beer collab of 2020.

ALD IPA hit ALDI shelves across the UK and Germany.

When competition gets messy, don't default to lawsuits. Default to creativity.

Because sometimes, the best way to beat the game—is to play along.

And partners are always a lot more valuable than rivals.

examples.meta: Tey Bannerman, 9,882 reactions / 1,006 comments, Aug 2025 (107-country AI values study)
Alex Wang, 3,463 reactions, Jul 2025 (McKinsey 150+ GenAI initiatives)

example_text:
There's something almost nobody is talking about in AI - but it affects everything from asking ChatGPT for advice to companies deploying AI globally.

A fascinating study tested major AI Models - the foundations powering tools millions use daily - against cultural values from 107 countries worldwide.

The result? Each one reflected the same assumptions - those of English-speaking, Western European societies. None aligned with how people in Africa, Latin America, or the Middle East actually build trust, show respect, or resolve conflicts.

Why does this matter? Imagine you're a global company rolling out AI customer service. Your system learns "best practice": when customers complain about late orders, "apologise briefly, offer a discount, and focus on quick resolution".

In Germany, the direct, efficient approach works perfectly. Customer satisfied.

But in Japan, that brief apology violates meiwaku - the cultural need to deeply acknowledge when you've caused someone inconvenience. Your "efficient" response feels dismissive and damages customer relationships.

And in the UAE, the discount offer backfires completely. It feels like charity rather than respect.

One AI system, similar contexts, completely different cultural outcomes.

This isn't intentional though - it's inevitable. LLMs absorb embedded patterns about communication from their training data, and most of that data comes from billions of English web pages and content. The result? AI systems that, unless thoughtfully shaped, are blind to the diversity of human interaction.

Klarna, the global payments company, made headlines in 2024 when they introduced an AI system that "did the work of 700 customer service reps", handled 2.5 million conversations in 35 languages, and cut response time by 82%. Technical triumph.

14 months later: "Klarna reverses AI strategy and is hiring humans again". Their CEO admitted it had led to "lower quality". Some reports said they'd seen a 20%+ decrease in customer satisfaction.

What I think really happened: Klarna optimised for 35 languages while completely missing 35 different ways humans expect to be treated.

The challenge? Most companies are focusing on technical integration and completely missing cultural intelligence. We measure response time and cost savings, but never ask, "which human complexities are we overlooking?"

The goal isn't neutrality though - that's impossible and undesirable. It's conscious awareness. Understanding that the output from AI models is filtered through a specific cultural lens.

For companies building AI strategies, key questions worth asking:

* Which cultural assumptions are embedded in our AI systems?
* How do we test cultural intelligence alongside technical performance?
* Who provides this expertise in our AI teams?

The individuals and organisations that develop this conscious awareness will make better decisions, while others unknowingly apply one-size-fits-all approaches to beautifully diverse human contexts.

Odun O., 908 reactions, Feb 2025 (turning down acquirers; customer-funded lessons)

example_text:
14 years at Google 🎂 Almost an eternity in Silicon Valley terms. ⏳ Looking back, I'm thinking about many of you who have reached out on LinkedIn, the hopefuls trying to carve out your career paths in this world. So, here's a moment to reflect and share some of my best advice for this next year... 🙂

➡️ The truth about AI: It feels like too many people - especially younger professionals - might be missing the point. While they're getting amazing with the actual tools, I see people becoming too reductive in the potential paths. Worried about replacement when they should be planning for acceleration in their careers. AI isn't coming for your economist job, your data science career or that UX gig. It's coming for the crushing grunt work that keeps you from the brilliant things that only humans can do: having an original thought, following a wild hypothesis, or connecting impossible dots into new innovations. In other words, please...please...don't be the one to limit yourself.

➡️ As for career-switchers: this might be a golden age. When AI-powered machines take over the repetitive, tedious parts of a role, like writing long emails, making slides and trudging through countless pages of research, suddenly the doors to creativity really open. I've watched people who would've sworn off ever working with a single line of syntax now diving in headfirst into vibe coding, expressing their unique view of the world through programming for the very first time. You still need the guts to cross that threshold, to think of your role more expansively.

➡️ Human connections matter more than ever. When every resume looks perfect and everyone interviews with GPT tools backing them up, people are going back to the oldest currency: who vouches for you. Did you know that half of Google's hires came from referrals at one point. Not because it's a magic ticket or something, but because great people know other great people. That's why every referral submission asks employees "How do you know this person?" As the process gets more competitive, get out there: conferences, hackathons, industry events - wherever your tribe gathers. Help others answer that question of how much they really know you. Human connection in an AI world. Isn't that a beautiful irony?

In other words, keep pushing. The road ahead will be awesome. 🛣️
